segments.text: AI can write code, explain chemistry, and help you outline an essay.
But how exactly did it learn to do these things?
Think about learning to shoot a basketball.
You take a shot, that's your guess.
You check where the ball goes, and then you adjust your aim or the force you use for your next attempt.
This diagram shows how AI training follows that exact same pattern.
But instead of adjusting physical force,
training adjusts the internal numbers inside the model to help it make a better guess next time.
Let's look at a specific training sample, the phrase peanut butter and jelly.
Given peanut butter and blank, the model initially guesses cloud.
Next, it checks that guess against the actual example, which says jelly.
The training process then adjusts the model's internal numbers to make jelly a more likely outcome.
By repeating this microscopic sequence, guess, check, adjust.
Across billions of text examples, the AI slowly builds up complex pattern recognition from scratch.
Before the guessing and checking loop starts, engineers must build the model's foundation.
This graphic details the initial setup.
On the left, engineers design the architecture of the model and assign all those internal numbers their starting values.
Meanwhile, teams collect a massive curriculum.
They gather books, websites, conversations, code, and media to serve as the actual training examples.
Because this curriculum serves as the model's entire world of information,
it can only learn the patterns, languages, and facts contained within these specific collections.
The actual training is split into three main phases.
We are going to track how each successive phase improves the model's response to one specific prompt.
How do I shoot a basketball?
As this chart illustrates, phase one is pre-training.
The model consumes vast amounts of text, repeatedly guesses what comes next,
and adjusts its internal munders, now officially called weights, based on the results.
If we ask it our basketball question right now, it replies,
the basketball shot is one of the most fundamental skills in the sport.
In this guide, we will cover the text flows perfectly, but it reads like the start of an article rather than following instructions.
This phase allows the model to mirror the structure of human language and store the facts found in its data,
though it still lacks the specific training needed to follow a user's instructions.
Phase two is instruction tuning.
Human trainers provide specific questions paired with ideal example answers.
The model practices aligning its guesses with these structured responses.
Pause the video for a second.
Think about how the model's answer will change.
Now that it's actively trying to follow instructions instead of just writing an article,
here is the updated response.
To shoot a basketball, square your feet to the hoop, bend your knees, and push up.
It now provides direct, actionable steps, because its weights have been adjusted to match the format of a helpful reply.
Yet, a limitation remains.
The model can adhere to the format of a request, but the actual advice it delivers might still be unclear or incomplete.
Instruction tuning successfully teaches the model how to answer a user,
but it does not guarantee it will generate the most useful advice possible.
That requires phase three, preference tuning.
Humans review several different answers generated by the model for a single question.
They rank them based on clarity, accuracy, and usefulness, adjusting the weights one last time.
The response now looks like this.
Great question.
Start close to the hoop.
Use one hand to shoot and the other to study the ball.
The friendly tone, logical structure, and practical advice are direct results of this human preference ranking.
Despite this rigorous feedback, a significant flaw persists.
The AI can still confidently generate a wrong answer that simply sounds correct.
Human feedback provides the final polish, turning a raw text predictor into the conversational, highly useful AI assistant we use today.
When preference tuning ends, the model is officially ready for the public.
This marks a hard boundary in the technology.
This animation illustrates a common misconception.
When you chat with an AI, your daily conversation does not change the model's weights.
The training phase is entirely over.
Every capability you see in the final product is the result of learning through billions of examples, followed by meticulous human feedback.
Guess, check, adjust, repeat.
